prompt: Match each point from the analyst unit with what the course text says about it.

pairs.right: Confirm with management that the benefits outweigh the costs
State the objectives, the data to store, the processing, and the outputs
Pick the solution with the fewest risks and most benefits

pairs.left: An information system, as an arrangement
pairs.right: People, data, processes and information technology
Source of requirements, labour that builds, ultimate users
Business objectives into functional requirements, jargon into plain terms

explanation: Six points from Module One Unit 1, each paired with the course text's own words.

prompt: True or false: the course text defines a system as a single component that works alone to achieve an outcome.
explanation: A system is a COLLECTION of INTERRELATED components that function TOGETHER to achieve some outcome.

why.true: Wrong. A system is many interrelated components working together.
why.false: Correct. The definition is a collection of interrelated components.

prompt: Match each term from the life cycle unit with what the course text attaches to it.

pairs.right: Building, deploying, using and updating an information system
Economic, organisational, technical, resource and schedule

pairs.left: Key words of the analysis phase
pairs.right: Discovery and understanding
Architecture, network, interfaces, database and system controls
Turning off the old system and turning on the new one
A training plan for users

explanation: Six anchors of the SDLC unit. Note that the planning-phase feasibility list on page 21 differs from the five-part list given for feasibility studies on page 24.

prompt: True or false: in the analysis phase, information is gathered only by reading existing documents; talking to users comes later.
explanation: Four sources, used together: observing users, interviewing them, reading existing documents, and reviewing existing automated systems.

why.true: Wrong. Observing and interviewing users are also gathering methods.
why.false: Correct. Users are observed and interviewed as well.

prompt: True or false: the objective of design is to design the solution system based on the requirements defined and decisions made during analysis.
explanation: Design builds on analysis: its requirements and its decisions.

why.true: Correct. That is the text's objective of design.
why.false: Wrong. The text states the objective exactly so.

prompt: What is the objective of the implementation phase, according to the course text?

options.text: To produce a reliable, fully functional system and ensure all users are trained to use it effectively
To identify the scope of the new system
To understand and document the business needs
To keep the system running for years after installation

explanation: A reliable, fully functional system, with trained users. Training is part of implementation, not an afterthought.

why.a: Correct. That is the implementation objective.
why.b: Wrong. That is a planning objective.
why.c: Wrong. That is the analysis objective.
why.d: Wrong. That is the support objective.

prompt: Match each point with the methodology, and the side, the course text puts it on.

pairs.right: An advantage of Waterfall

pairs.left: Verification and validation are done early
pairs.right: An advantage of the V-Shaped Model
A disadvantage of the V-Shaped Model

pairs.left: Each release delivers an operational product
pairs.right: An advantage of the Incremental model

pairs.left: Hard to map requirements to increments of the right size
pairs.right: A disadvantage of the Incremental model

pairs.left: Customers can see requirements as they are gathered
pairs.right: An advantage of evolutionary prototyping
A disadvantage of evolutionary prototyping

explanation: Advantages and disadvantages are the most examined lists in the unit. Learn each one BESIDE its methodology.

prompt: Match each item with the course text's description.

pairs.right: Structured approaches, models and techniques for every phase
Used to structure, plan and control development
By the approval committee and the project sponsor
Documentation, formal reviews, and sign-off at each phase end
A quick and dirty version with minimal features
A thorough analysis phase
A working increment for user evaluation

explanation: Definitions and mechanisms of the methodologies unit, each in the text's words.

prompt: Match each heading with its list from the course text.

pairs.right: Reusable components, visual tools and intensive user involvement
Requirements fairly well known, low technical risk, no high performance needed
Build, demonstrate, the user evaluates and suggests, repeat
Unstable requirements, user interfaces, short-lived demonstrations
User stories, sprint planning, development and testing, review and retrospective
Requirements clarity, technology familiarity, complexity, reliability, short schedules, schedule visibility

explanation: Six lists that the objective section likes to test as 'which of these belongs to...'.

prompt: What does the course text say often happens when information systems are developed WITHOUT a clear methodology?

options.text: Cost overruns, missed deadlines, and systems that fail to meet user and business requirements

explanation: Three failures: cost, time, and requirements not met.

why.a: Wrong. The text gives real consequences.
why.c: Wrong. The text warns of the opposite.
why.d: Wrong. Not what the text says.

prompt: True or false: the Spiral model is one of the five methodologies covered in the methodologies unit.
explanation: The five covered are Waterfall, RAD, Prototyping, the Incremental model and Agile. Spiral appears only in the life cycle unit, as the example of an adaptive approach.

why.true: Wrong. Spiral is the SDLC unit's adaptive example, not one of the five.
why.false: Correct. It is not among the five.

prompt: What does the course text call the FIRST challenge for project managers?
explanation: Selecting the methodology, which is not simple because no one methodology is always best.

why.a: Wrong. Not named as the first challenge.
why.d: Wrong. A data model is independent of the database product anyway.

prompt: Match each term with its meaning in the fact gathering unit.

pairs.right: Identifying and extracting problems and requirements from the user community
Problem discovery, requirements discovery, documenting and analysing, management
What the system should do and the conditions it must operate under
During the analysis phase
A contract for the project, in business language
Lost credibility, legal liability, possibly a lost job

explanation: The vocabulary of requirements, one pair at a time.

prompt: Match each item with what the course text says about it.

pairs.right: Do not misuse sensitive information, and protect it
Facial disclosure, eye contact and posture
Sponsor, facilitator, users and managers, scribes, IT staff
Encourage participation without letting individuals dominate
Many ideas fast, no analysis until all are exhausted
Less time needed to develop systems

explanation: Ethics, interviewing and JRP, the parts of the unit asked as lists.

prompt: True or false: the course text defines a problem as an undesirable situation that prevents the organisation from fully achieving its mission, vision, goals and objectives.
explanation: That is the definition, word for word in substance.

why.true: Correct. The text's definition of a problem.
why.false: Wrong. This is exactly how the text defines a problem.

prompt: Which skills does the course text say requirements discovery requires?
explanation: Analytical, communication and interpersonal: listen, ask the right questions, resolve conflicts, validate findings.

why.b: Wrong. Not the skills named for discovery.

prompt: True or false: non-functional requirements are what the information system must DO.
explanation: Functional requirements are what the system must DO; non-functional requirements are what it must HAVE.

why.true: Wrong. What it must DO is functional.
why.false: Correct. Non-functional is what it must HAVE.

prompt: True or false: 'functional specifications' is one of the other names for the requirements definition document.
explanation: Also: requirements definition report, requirements statement, requirements specification.

why.true: Correct. It is one of the names.
why.false: Wrong. The text lists it among the other names.

prompt: What does sampling existing documents give the analyst insight into, according to the course text?

options.text: Current business processes, business rules and information requirements

explanation: Processes, rules and information requirements, and it exposes redundancies, inconsistencies and data quality issues.

why.b: Wrong. Opinions come from questionnaires and interviews.
why.d: Wrong. That is a design decision.

prompt: A questionnaire asks respondents to rank five features in order of importance. What type of questionnaire is this?
explanation: Ranking questions, like multiple-choice and rating questions, are fixed-format: the respondent chooses from predefined responses.

why.a: Wrong. Free-format lets the respondent write their own answer.
why.b: Correct. Ranking is a fixed-format question type.
why.d: Wrong. Open-ended describes an interview question.

prompt: In a structured interview, the analyst asks 'Tell me how you handle a customer complaint.' What kind of question is this?
explanation: Open-ended: the interviewee may respond in any way. A closed-ended question would restrict the answer to choices or a short reply.

why.d: Wrong. Ranking is a fixed-format questionnaire item.

prompt: What is the purpose of following up on an interview?

options.text: To validate the documented responses with the interviewee or stakeholders and avoid misunderstandings
To ask for a salary increase
To start the next interview immediately

explanation: Validation makes the gathered information reliable.

why.c: Wrong. Follow-up is about this interview's results.
why.d: Wrong. Notes are kept and reviewed.

prompt: According to the brainstorming guidelines, WHEN should the ideas be analysed and evaluated?

options.text: As each idea is called out
Only after the group has run out of ideas and all have been recorded
Before the session, by the manager

explanation: Call ideas out fast, record them all, and only then analyse, evaluate, refine, combine and improve.

why.a: Wrong. Analysis during generation kills ideas.
why.b: Correct. Only after the ideas run out.
why.c: Wrong. The ideas do not exist yet.
why.d: Wrong. They are evaluated, just at the end.

prompt: Match each use-case term with the course text's description.

pairs.right: User activities and the system's responses
External or functional, not internal
They capture most functional requirements and expose exceptions
The use case diagram and the narrative
A step-by-step textual description

pairs.left: First step to produce a use-case model
pairs.right: Identify the business actors

explanation: The core of the use case unit in six pairs.

prompt: True or false: postconditions are one of the basic elements of a use case narrative.
explanation: Name and identifier, actors, description, preconditions, main flow, alternative flows, postconditions.

why.false: Wrong. They are one of the elements.

prompt: At the ATM the customer enters an invalid PIN. Which part of the use case narrative describes what happens next?
explanation: Alternative flows describe variations, exceptions and errors that branch off the main flow, such as an invalid PIN or insufficient funds.

why.a: Wrong. The main flow is the ideal scenario where everything works.
why.c: Wrong. Preconditions are true before the use case starts.
why.d: Wrong. Postconditions are true after it completes.

prompt: True or false: 'Who will maintain information in the system?' is one of the questions for finding USE CASES.
explanation: That is one of the questions for finding ACTORS. The use case questions are about the actor's main tasks and the information passing between actor and system.

why.true: Wrong. It is an actor-finding question.
why.false: Correct. It belongs to the actor questions.

prompt: Match each process modelling term with the course text's description.

pairs.right: How a business system should operate, and how data moves among its processes
The new system being developed
Processes and the data between them, with no programming detail

pairs.left: What DFDs let the analyst determine
pairs.right: What the organisation does and how
The DFD notation the course text uses
Going from one system to many component processes
Conserving inputs and outputs across levels

explanation: The vocabulary of process modelling, seven pairs.

prompt: True or false: the course text defines a model as a pictorial representation of reality.
explanation: A model is a picture of reality; a process model pictures a business system.

why.false: Wrong. The text defines a model exactly so.

prompt: True or false: one reason process modelling matters is that DFDs allow parts of the system to be isolated at any chosen level of detail.
explanation: Isolation at any level is one of the six reasons, with business focus, understanding requirements, cheap modification, readable notation and formal documentation.

why.true: Correct. It is one of the reasons.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the course text's hints that something is a logical process?

options.text: It sorts, filters or summarises data
It holds data at rest for later use

explanation: Holding data at rest is a DATA STORE. The process hints: computes, decides, sorts or summarises, organises data into information, triggers processes, uses stored data.

why.a: Wrong choice, because computing IS a process hint.
why.b: Wrong choice, because sorting and summarising IS a process hint.
why.c: Correct. That describes a data store, not a process.
why.d: Wrong choice, because triggering other processes IS a hint.

prompt: Match each data modelling term with the course text's description.

pairs.right: Usually the first step in database design; it produces an ERD
The same design in Access, MySQL or any other system
Business rules exposed before they are buried in code
An attribute broken into smaller ones, like Address
One relationship line at a time, in both directions

pairs.left: Student and Course in the worked example
pairs.right: Many-to-many, through Registers for

explanation: Data modelling in six pairs.

prompt: Which property of a relationship line states whether the relationship is mandatory or optional?
explanation: Link phrase is the verb, cardinality is how many, ordinality is must or may.

why.a: Wrong. The link phrase is the verb.
why.d: Wrong. The identifier is an attribute, not a line property.

prompt: True or false: the course text gives FOUR common cardinal relationships.
explanation: Three: one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many.

prompt: One customer can place many orders, but each order belongs to only one customer. What is the cardinality?
explanation: This is the text's own one-to-many example. One-to-one is the employee and login account.

why.a: Wrong. One-to-one is the employee and login account example.
why.c: Wrong. An order belongs to only one customer.
why.d: Wrong. That is ordinality language, not a cardinality.

prompt: Match each object-oriented idea with the course text's description.

pairs.right: Process and data combined in one object
By sending messages, calling one another's operations
Check the classes against the use cases
Iterative, with gaps fed back
A notation, not a method

explanation: Five anchors of the object orientation unit.

prompt: True or false: an object is a single instance of something in the system, such as a particular order.
explanation: One particular student or order is an object; the class is the blueprint for all of them.

why.false: Wrong. The text defines an object exactly so.

prompt: Match each item with the course text's description.

pairs.right: Classes, attributes, operations and relationships
Its attributes
The small symbol at one end of the line

pairs.left: First step to build a class diagram
pairs.right: Identify candidate classes from the requirements model

pairs.left: Enrolment in the worked class diagram
pairs.right: The associative class
A behavioural diagram
Both are drawn as dashed arrows

explanation: The structural and use-case modelling unit in seven pairs.

prompt: True or false: Record Grades INCLUDES Save Grades, because every act of recording grades must end with saving them.
explanation: Include means always required: that is the text's own example.

why.false: Wrong. This is the text's example of include.

prompt: True or false: when building a use case diagram, include and extend relationships are identified FIRST, before the actors.
explanation: They come LAST: identify actors, identify use cases, draw association lines, then add include or extend relationships.

why.true: Wrong. Actors come first; include and extend come last.
why.false: Correct. They are the final step.

prompt: True or false: in a sequence diagram, messages are ordered from top to bottom to show the sequence.
explanation: Time runs down the page along the lifelines.

why.false: Wrong. The text orders messages top to bottom.

prompt: True or false: a component cannot be replaced once built, even by another implementation that honours the same interface.
explanation: A component is replaceable and self-contained: any alternative implementation that honours the same interface can take its place.

why.true: Wrong. Replaceability is part of the definition.
why.false: Correct. Components are replaceable behind their interface.

prompt: True or false: sequence diagrams are more useful than collaboration diagrams when the focus is on the exact timing and order of messages.
explanation: Sequence for timing and order; collaboration for how objects are structurally connected.

why.true: Correct. Timing and order favour the sequence diagram.
why.false: Wrong. The text says exactly this.
